question.problem: The mean number of bacteria per milliliter of a liquid is $6.$ What is the probability that there will be no more than $3$ bacteria in one milliliter of the liquid? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places. You may assume that bacteria appear independently and at a constant average rate.
question.worked_solution:
A Poisson random variable $X$ with rate $\lambda $ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=\frac{{\lambda }^{x}{e}^{-\lambda }}{x!}
$$

Let $X$ be the number of bacteria in one milliliter of the liquid. Since the average rate is $6$ bacteria per milliliter, and events occur independently and at a constant average rate, the number of bacteria can be modeled as a Poisson random variable with rate $\lambda =6,$ and we can write $X∼\text{Po}(6).$

So, $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=\frac{{6}^{x}{e}^{-6}}{x!}
$$

Therefore, the probability that at most $3$ bacteria will be found in one milliliter of the liquid is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 3) & =P(X\in \{0,1,2,3\}) \\  & =f(0)+f(1)+f(2)+f(3) \\  & =\frac{{6}^{0}{e}^{-6}}{0!}+\frac{{6}^{1}{e}^{-6}}{1!}+\frac{{6}^{2}{e}^{-6}}{2!}+\frac{{6}^{3}{e}^{-6}}{3!} \\  & ≈0.151\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.
